title: Family and age
title_target: 你家有几口人 — Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén
goal: Name family members, count the people in your household, ask someone's age in three different ways depending on who you're talking to, and join two nouns with 和.
bekal: name father, mother, older and younger siblings, and children
answer 你家有几口人 correctly
ask the age of a child, a peer, and an older person with the right form
use 和 only where it belongs
say someone's age with no verb at all

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — A family photo
dialogs.intro: Wang Li shows Andi a photo of her family. Notice one odd thing about the sentences with ages: the verb disappears completely.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: This is a photo of my family.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How many people are in your family?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [五|Wǔ][口|kǒu][人|rén]。[爸爸|Bàba]、[妈妈|māma]、[哥哥|gēge]、[妹妹|mèimei][和|hé][我|wǒ]。
lines.id: Five. My dad, my mom, my older brother, my younger sister, and me.
lines.literal: five — (measure) — person. dad, mom, older-brother, younger-sister — and — I.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: What does your brother do?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: He's a doctor. He's thirty this year.
lines.literal: he — is — doctor. he — this-year — thirty — years-old.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How old is your sister?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: She's sixteen, still in high school.
lines.literal: she — sixteen — years-old, still — is — middle-school-student.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: What about your parents? Do they work?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][爸爸|bàba][还|hái][工作|gōngzuò]，[我|wǒ][妈妈|māma][退休|tuìxiū][了|le]。
lines.id: My dad still works; my mom has retired.
lines.literal: I — dad — still — work, I — mom — retire — (change).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Do you all live in Beijing?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [不|Bù]，[他们|tāmen][住|zhù][在|zài][上海|Shànghǎi]。[我|Wǒ][一个人|yí ge rén][在|zài][北京|Běijīng]。
lines.id: No, they live in Shanghai. I'm on my own in Beijing.
lines.literal: no, they — live — at — Shanghai. I — one — (measure) — person — be-at — Beijing.

notes: **⚠️ [口|kǒu] is a special measure word for counting the people in a household**, and only for that. [我家有五口人|Wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén]. Outside the family, people are counted with [个|ge]: [三个学生|sān ge xuésheng]. Using 个 for family isn't a big mistake, but using 口 for people outside the family sounds odd.

**⚠️ Age sentences use no verb at all.** [他三十岁|Tā sānshí suì] — literally “he thirty years-old”. There's no 是 in it. Adding 是 (他是三十岁) is a mistake people notice at once — and a tempting one, since English says “he *is* thirty”. This is one of the few Mandarin sentences that truly stands without a verb.

**⚠️ [和|hé] “and” only joins NOUNS**, never two sentences or two actions. Right: [爸爸和妈妈|bàba hé māma]. Wrong: 我吃饭和我看书 — two actions are joined without 和, just separated by a comma or linked with [然后|ránhòu] “then”.
**[还|hái] = still.** [他还工作|Tā hái gōngzuò] he still works; [她还是中学生|Tā hái shì zhōngxuéshēng] she's still in high school.
**[退休了|tuìxiū le] = has retired.** 了 here marks a **change of state**: she used to work, now she doesn't. That's the real job of 了 — not marking the past. Unit 10 covers it fully.
**[一个人|yí ge rén] means “on my own, alone”**, not “one person” as a count. [我一个人去|Wǒ yí ge rén qù] = I'm going alone.
**[住在|zhù zài] = live in.** Notice the order: the verb 住 first, then 在 + place. We'll cover 在 fully in Unit 6.

grammars.title: Asking someone's age — three forms, three kinds of people
body: English uses one sentence for everyone: “how old are you?”. Mandarin changes the question depending on who you're asking, and using the wrong one is quite noticeable.

head: Answering
Example
rows: [我今年二十五岁|Wǒ jīnnián èrshíwǔ suì]。

after: ⚠️ [多大|duō dà] literally means “how big”, so don't be surprised: the same phrase is also used to ask about the size of things. Who you're talking about decides the meaning.
The pattern [多|duō] + adjective = “how …” is very productive: [多高|duō gāo] how tall, [多长|duō cháng] how long, [多远|duō yuǎn] how far, [多重|duō zhòng] how heavy.

grammars.title: 和 and friends — ways of joining things

head: Word
Joins
Example
rows: [我和我妹妹|wǒ hé wǒ mèimei] my sister and I
Same as 和, more spoken; also “with”
[我跟他去|Wǒ gēn tā qù] I'm going with him
Adds the last item to a list
[苹果、香蕉，还有水|píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo, háiyǒu shuǐ]
[我吃饭，然后看书|Wǒ chī fàn, ránhòu kàn shū]

after: ⚠️ A mistake you'll almost certainly make this week: using 和 to join two sentences, as in “I eat **and** read a book”. In Mandarin, two actions are just separated by a comma. **和 never stands between two verbs.**
Notice Mandarin list punctuation too: the slanted comma [、|dùnhào] goes between items in a list, while the ordinary comma ，goes between parts of a sentence.

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — Asking about each other's families
dialogs.intro: Now it's Li Ming's turn to ask Andi. Talking about family is the most common small talk in China — far more common than talking about the weather.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Andi, are you married?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Yes. I have a daughter.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: How old is she now?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Six. She's in elementary school in Jakarta.
lines.literal: six — years-old. she — at — Jakarta — attend — elementary-school.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Is your wife in Indonesia too?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Yes. I miss them a lot.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Yes, a younger brother. He's five years younger than me.
lines.literal: have, one — (measure) — younger-brother. he — compared-to — I — small — five — years.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][是|shì][独生子|dúshēngzǐ]。[家里|Jiā li][只有|zhǐyǒu][我|wǒ][一个|yí ge][孩子|háizi]。
lines.id: I'm an only child. I'm the only kid at home.
lines.literal: I — am — only-born-son. home — inside — only-have — I — one — (measure) — child.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Then your parents must really dote on you.
lines.literal: then — you — parents — surely — (support) — dote-on — you.

notes: **[结婚了吗|Jiéhūn le ma]？ — “are you married?”** This question is genuinely common in China, even with people you've just met. It isn't considered nosy; it's considered caring. Short answers: [结婚了|Jiéhūn le] or [还没有|Hái méiyǒu] “not yet”.
**[几岁了|Jǐ suì le]？** — the 了 at the end adds a sense of “by now”, as if asking about an age that keeps growing. Very common with children.
**[上小学|shàng xiǎoxué] = be in elementary school.** 上 here means “go up to, attend”: [上班|shàng bān] go to work, [上课|shàng kè] go to class, [上大学|shàng dàxué] go to university.

**[想|xiǎng] has two meanings: “would like” and “miss”.** [我想去|Wǒ xiǎng qù] I'd like to go; [我想你|Wǒ xiǎng nǐ] I miss you. The difference: followed by a **verb**, it means “would like”; followed by a **person**, it means “miss”.
**[比|bǐ] = compared with.** The pattern is A 比 B + adjective: [他比我大|Tā bǐ wǒ dà] he's older than me. ⚠️ Don't use 很 in a 比 sentence — [他比我很大|Tā bǐ wǒ hěn dà] is wrong.
**[独生子|dúshēngzǐ] only son, [独生女|dúshēngnǚ] only daughter.** Very common words in China because of the one-child policy, in force from 1979 to 2015.
**[疼|téng] means “ache, hurt”, but also “dote on”** — with a sense of spoiling. [父母很疼他|Fùmǔ hěn téng tā] his parents really dote on him.

grammars.title: 比 — comparing two things
body: This pattern is officially HSK 3 material, but it's placed here because you'll need it as soon as you talk about age and family.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: [他比我大五岁|Tā bǐ wǒ dà wǔ suì]。
He's five years older than me.
I'm not as tall as him.
A 跟 B 一样 + adjective
[我跟他一样大|Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng dà]。
I'm the same age as him.

after: ⚠️ **很 and 比 never meet.** The support word 很 disappears as soon as there's a comparison. To say “much more”, add [多|duō] or [得多|de duō] after: [他比我大得多|Tā bǐ wǒ dà de duō].

blocks.text: Mandarin distinguishes siblings by **age** — there is no single word for “brother” or “sister”, only older and younger ones. And it goes further: grandparents on your father's side and your mother's side have different names.

head: Mandarin
Pīnyīn
Meaning
rows: uncle (father's younger brother); also a way to address adult men
aunt (mother's sister); also a way to address adult women

blocks.title: 外 — the “mother's side” marker
items: The character [外|wài] means “outside”. It goes in front of family terms on the **mother's side**: [外公|wàigōng], [外婆|wàipó], [外孙|wàisūn] a daughter's child.
The reason is historical: the traditional Chinese family traced descent through the father's line, so the mother's side was literally “outside” the surname.
Today it's only a trace in the language, not a family attitude — but the words are still used exactly as before.
**[叔叔|shūshu] and [阿姨|āyí] are also used for strangers** around your parents' age, much like a child calling a family friend “auntie” or “uncle”.

blocks.text: A first conversation with someone from China almost always runs through these questions. To many Western ears some of them feel personal; to them, this is simply friendliness.

head: Question
Meaning
Safe answer
rows: [你家有几口人|Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén]？
How many people in your family?
[有一个|Yǒu yí ge]。 / [还没有|Hái méiyǒu]。
[我是雅加达人|Wǒ shì Yǎjiādá rén]。
[你父母做什么工作|Nǐ fùmǔ zuò shénme gōngzuò]？
[我爸爸是老师|Wǒ bàba shì lǎoshī]。
[你一个月挣多少钱|Nǐ yí ge yuè zhèng duōshao qián]？
How much do you earn a month?
[还行吧|Hái xíng ba]。 — a polite dodge

blocks.title: If you'd rather not answer
items: **[还行吧|Hái xíng ba]。** — “It's OK.” A neutral answer to questions about money or work.
**[保密|Bǎomì]！** — “It's a secret!” Said with a smile; taken as funny, not rude.
**[还没有|Hái méiyǒu]。** — “Not yet.” For questions about marriage or children. People rarely push further.
Turning the question around with [你呢|Nǐ ne]？ almost always works and offends no one.

items: [他是三十岁|Tā shì sānshí suì]。

answers: 口 — 个 — 岁 — 和 — 比
几岁 — 多大 — 多大年纪 — 几岁 — 多大
